extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic theory, institutional design, and political reform
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria about how democratic institutions should gather information, represent interests, and exercise power; critiques of guild socialism and shop/function-based representation. Useful for analyzing institutional design, representation schemes, and the role of information in public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled reporting and objective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: "They can be known only by controlled reporting and objective analysis."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws' real effects are subtle and hidden and cannot be understood by filtering local experiences through local states of mind; lawmakers need systematic instruments (analogous to an accountant's cost sheets) rather than relying on a mosaic of local pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for instruments to calibrate local impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature cannot arrive at a true picture of the state of the union by putting together a mosaic of local pictures; "unless he possesses instruments for calibrating them, one picture is as good as the next."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressmen need institutional tools for calibrating and comparing local reports; without these, local impressions are insufficient as a base for national policy or foreign policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of one-sided executive reporting and press leaks
rubrics_metrics.description: "The President... tells Congress what he chooses to tell it. He cannot be heckled, and the censorship as to what is compatible with the public interest is in his hands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because executive communications are selective and unchallenged, Congress is forced to rely on private tips, newspapers, or investigative eruptions; this asymmetry distorts legislative knowledge and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional investigations as a flawed substitute for steady information
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is often "forced to rely either on private tips or on that legalized atrocity, the Congressional investigation" when legitimate steady information is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad hoc investigations are sensational, inefficient, and produce limited useful information; sustained, objective reporting and expert assistance are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of expert bodies and specialized reporting for national legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful channels include "occasional communications from the executive departments, interested and disinterested data collected by private persons... and a new and excellent practice of calling for help from expert bodies like the Interstate Commerce Commission, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Tariff Commission."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation of a national character requires input from expert commissions and organized data collection to avoid incestuous or parochial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of localism: logrolling and parceling national law into local items
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of effective information and analysis, legislation tends to be "broken up into a collection of local items, each of which is enacted for a local reason" producing tariff schedules, navy yards, post offices, pensions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such parceling creates pork-barrel politics and logrolling, where lawmakers vote for narrow local benefits rather than coherent national policy; representation that is only locally informed will produce this outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative limitations: specialization and delegation are inevitable
rubrics_metrics.description: "The cleverest and most industrious representative cannot hope to understand a fraction of the bills on which he votes. The best he can do is to specialize on a few bills, and take somebody's word about the rest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize practical limits on individual legislators' knowledge; institutional provision should ensure reliable, accessible information rather than forcing legislators to dig for facts themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-coercive society still requires institutions to maintain equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although guild socialists seek "a new society which will be conceived in the spirit, not of coercion, but of free service," they "are too honest to shirk the element of force required to make the transition" and must provide "institutions for maintaining" an equilibrium if equality is to be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-coercive ideal does not eliminate the need for institutional mechanisms (and possibly coercive measures during transition) to secure and maintain egalitarian outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers required of a central coordinating body (the Commune) in guild proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commune (federalized into local/provincial and National communes) is described as settling price disputes, fixing prices at times, allocating surplus or distributing loss, allocating natural resources, controlling credit, allocating communal labor-power, ratifying guild budgets and by-laws, levying taxes, allocating income, appointing judges, conferring coercive powers on guilds, declaring war and making peace, controlling armed forces, and representing the nation abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although presented as non-sovereign, this list of powers is effectively sovereign and coercive; any scheme that vests these functions centrally must confront the reality of coercion and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory/shop as the natural unit of industrial democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The guildsmen identify the factory (broadly: "mines, shipyards, docks, stations, and every place which is 'a natural center of production'")—more precisely, the shop—as the "natural and fundamental unit of industrial democracy" where men can be in personal contact and self-government exercised directly by each member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For functional democracy to be meaningful it must operate at a scale small enough for direct knowledge; however, the smaller unit's internal democracy is necessarily limited by dependencies on larger structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of shop democracy for external and translocal affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-government in the shop covers matters "that can be taken in at a single view," but disputes arise about what is internal; big issues like wages, standards of production, marketing, and broader planning are "by no means purely internal" and the shop "is thoroughly entangled in foreign affairs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shop-level democracy cannot by itself determine relations to plant, industry, or nation; federated representative structures and informed coordination mechanisms are required to manage external relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional representation: acting for 'particular functions' not groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild theory proposes that the only possible representative is one who acts for "some particular function," so "each person must help choose as many representatives 'as there are distinct essential groups of functions to be performed.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional representatives are supposed to vote according to specialized daily experience, but this presumes clear, recognized functions and risks leaving many questions outside the direct experience of any single function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency of functional democracy on a settled scheme of functions and an instructed electorate
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional democracy assumes "a society in which all the main work of the world has been analysed into functions, and these functions in turn synthesized harmoniously," and that the votes of the 'instructed' will reveal interest and define function while the 'uninstructed' waive their rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This depends on agreement about what counts as distinct essential functions and on sufficient civic education; absent these, functional voting becomes vulnerable to organized interests, machine politics, or the government's imposition of function definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic fallacy: focus on origin of power rather than its exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic fallacy is described as being "preoccupied with the origin of government rather than with the processes and results," assuming that deriving power in the 'right' way will make it beneficent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What determines the quality of civilization is how power is exercised, not merely how it is sourced; controlling the origin (the 'source') without institutions for transparent decision-making and reporting risks making vital decisions invisible and empowers a specialized, unaccountable class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common interests elude public opinion without institutions and education
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the absence of institutions and education by which the environment is so successfully reported that the realities of public life stand out sharply against self-centered opinion, the common interests very largely elude public opinion entirely, and can be managed only by a specialized class whose personal interests reach beyond the locality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion alone cannot form coherent common interests; reliable reporting, analysis, and public education are prerequisites so that citizens can conceive of and judge translocal or national issues rather than leaving them to an expert or specialized class.
